stem: A 2-year-old girl has a febrile convulsion lasting 4 minutes; her parents ask whether they should give paracetamol straight away next time to prevent another convulsion, what is the best response?

options.text: Yes, because antipyretics prevent the temperature from rising quickly
Yes, because antipyretics reduce the risk of later epilepsy
No, because antipyretics do not help febrile convulsions
No, because antipyretics worsen seizure duration
No, because antipyretics should never be used for fever in children

explanation: No, because antipyretics do not help febrile convulsions. Paracetamol may reduce discomfort from fever, but it does not prevent a febrile convulsion from occurring.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Paroxysmal Disorders

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because antipyretics do not prevent febrile convulsions by stopping the temperature from rising quickly.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because antipyretics do not reduce the risk of later epilepsy in this context.
optionExplanations.C: Correct because antipyretics do not help febrile convulsions, so giving paracetamol straight away does not prevent the seizure.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because the issue is lack of preventive benefit, not worsening seizure duration.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because antipyretics can still be used for fever symptoms; they simply do not prevent febrile convulsions.
